title: Public Health and Risk Communication During COVID-19—Enhancing Psychological Needs to Promote Sustainable Behavior Change
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how public health and risk communication during the COVID-19 pandemic can better support sustained behavior change in the face of misinformation, uncertainty, and public mistrust. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention experimentally, the authors develop a conceptual framework grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and related ideas from psychology, philosophy, and human-computer interaction to explain why some communication strategies are more likely to promote durable adherence to public health guidance.

The paper proposes five practical communication guidelines: create an autonomy-supportive climate, provide choice within constraints, use a bottom-up/co-production approach, create solidarity, and be transparent while acknowledging uncertainty. The discussion is illustrated through the case of public messaging about face coverings, and the authors integrate findings from a systematic search of COVID-19 communication literature to support the proposed principles.

The context is the general public during the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in relation to governmental and health-authority messaging in diverse national settings. The main conclusion is that communication strategies that respect autonomy, build competence, and foster relatedness are more likely to improve trust, adherence, and well-being than top-down, controlling, or opaque messaging. The paper emphasizes that effective communication should be actionable, inclusive, culturally sensitive, and transparent about both evidence and uncertainty.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a narrative/theoretical framework article with a small systematic literature search, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. It does not present a controlled design, effect estimates, or education-specific outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate an educational or AI intervention, so there is no measurable educational impact to code. Its contribution is conceptual guidance for public-health communication, not evidence of impact on K-12 outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing five public-health communication guidelines for COVID-19 rather than evaluating an AI or educational intervention. It synthesizes 20 emerging COVID-19 communication papers and argues that autonomy-supportive, bottom-up, solidarity-building, and transparent messaging may improve adherence to public-health guidance, but it does not report a quantitative effect size or experimental estimate.
finding.measure: Qualitative/theoretical synthesis of public health communication strategies; narrative review of included COVID-19 communication papers
